title: I. The Beginning Of Perhotin’s Official Career
paragraphs: Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, whom we left knocking at the sturdy locked gates of the widow Morozov's house, of course ended up making himself heard. Fenya, who was still shaken by the fright she had had two hours before, and too “upset” to go to bed, was almost driven into hysterics by the furious knocking at the gate. Even though she had seen him drive away with her own eyes, she imagined it must be Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocking again—no one else could pound so savagely. She ran to the house-porter, who had already woken and gone out to the gate, and began begging him not to open it. But once he'd questioned Pyotr Ilyitch and learned that he wanted to see Fenya on very “important business,” the man finally made up his mind to open up. Pyotr Ilyitch was admitted into Fenya's kitchen, but the girl asked him to let the house-porter stay, “because of her misgivings.” He began questioning her and at once learned the crucial fact: when Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run out to look for Grushenka, he had snatched up a pestle from the mortar, and when he returned, the pestle was gone and his hands were smeared with blood.

“And the blood was just flowing, dripping from him, dripping!” Fenya kept exclaiming. This horrible detail was really just the product of her disordered imagination. But although it hadn't been “dripping,” Pyotr Ilyitch had seen those blood-stained hands himself and had helped to wash them. Besides, the question he had to settle wasn't how soon the blood had dried, but where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run with the pestle—or rather, whether it really was to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, and how he could satisfactorily confirm it. Pyotr Ilyitch kept returning to this point, and though he found nothing conclusive, he came away with the conviction that Dmitri Fyodorovitch could have gone nowhere except his father's house, and that therefore something must have happened there.

“And when he came back,” Fenya added excitedly, “I told him the whole story, and then I began asking him, ‘Why do you have blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?' and he answered that it was human blood, and that he had just killed someone. He confessed it all to me, and suddenly ran off like a madman. I sat down and began thinking, where's he running off to now like a madman? He'll go to Mokroe, I thought, and kill my mistress there. I ran out to beg him not to kill her. I was running to his lodgings, but I looked at Plotnikov's shop and saw him just setting off, and there was no blood on his hands then.” (Fenya had noticed this and remembered it.) Fenya's old grandmother confirmed her testimony as well as she could. After asking a few more questions, Pyotr Ilyitch left the house even more upset and uneasy than when he'd entered.

The most direct and easiest thing for him to do would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, find out whether anything had happened there, and if so, what; and then to go to the police captain, as Pyotr Ilyitch firmly intended to do once he'd satisfied himself of the facts. But the night was dark, Fyodor Pavlovitch's gates were strong, and he would have to knock again. His acquaintance with Fyodor Pavlovitch was slight, and what if, after he'd been knocking, they opened to him and nothing had happened? Then Fyodor Pavlovitch, in his jeering way, would tell the story all over town—how a stranger called Perhotin had broken in on him at midnight to ask if anyone had killed him. It would make a scandal. And scandal was what Pyotr Ilyitch dreaded more than anything in the world.

Still, the feeling that had hold of him was so strong that, though he stamped his foot angrily and swore at himself, he set off again—not to Fyodor Pavlovitch's, but to Madame Hohlakov's. He decided that if she denied having just given Dmitri Fyodorovitch three thousand roubles, he would go straight to the police captain; but if she admitted having given him the money, he would go home and let the matter rest until morning.

It is, of course, perfectly obvious that there was even more potential for scandal in going at eleven o'clock at night to a fashionable lady, a complete stranger, and perhaps rousing her from her bed to ask her an amazing question, than in going to Fyodor Pavlovitch's. But that's just how it sometimes goes, especially in cases like this one, with the decisions of the most precise and phlegmatic people. Pyotr Ilyitch was by no means phlegmatic at that moment. He remembered all his life how a nagging unease gradually took hold of him, growing more and more painful and driving him on against his will. Of course, he kept cursing himself the whole way for going to this lady, but “I'll get to the bottom of it, I will!” he repeated for the tenth time, grinding his teeth, and he carried out his intention.

It was exactly eleven o'clock when he entered Madame Hohlakov's house. He was admitted into the yard fairly quickly, but when he asked whether the lady was still up, the porter could give no answer, except that she was usually in bed by that hour.
“Ask at the top of the stairs. If the lady wants to receive you, she'll receive you. If she doesn't, she won't.”

Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but he didn't find things so easy there. The footman was unwilling to announce him, but eventually called a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch politely but insistently begged her to tell her lady that an official living in town, named Perhotin, had called on particular business, and that if it hadn't been of the greatest importance, he wouldn't have ventured to come. “Tell her in those words, in those words exactly,” he urged the girl.

She went away. He stayed waiting in the entry. Madame Hohlakov was already in her bedroom, though not yet asleep. She had felt upset ever since Mitya's visit and had a premonition that she wouldn't get through the night without the sick headache that always followed such excitement in her. She was surprised when the maid announced her visitor. She refused irritably to see him, though the unexpected arrival at such an hour of “an official living in town,” a total stranger, stirred her feminine curiosity intensely. But this time Pyotr Ilyitch was stubborn as a mule. He begged the maid most earnestly to deliver another message, in these very words:
“That he had come on business of the greatest importance, and that Madame Hohlakov might have cause to regret it later if she refused to see him now.”
“I plunged headlong,” he described it afterwards.

The maid, gazing at him in amazement, went to deliver his message again. Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought for a little, asked what he looked like, and learned that he was “very well dressed, young, and so polite.” We may note, parenthetically, that Pyotr Ilyitch was a rather good-looking young man, and well aware of the fact. Madame Hohlakov decided to see him. She was in her dressing gown and slippers, but she flung a black shawl over her shoulders. “The official” was asked to walk into the drawing room—the very room where Mitya had been received a short while before. The lady came out to meet her visitor with a sternly inquiring expression and, without inviting him to sit down, began at once with the question:
“What do you want?”
“I have ventured to disturb you, madam, on a matter concerning our common acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov,” Perhotin began.
But he had scarcely uttered the name before the lady's face showed signs of acute irritation. She almost shrieked and interrupted him in a fury:

“How much longer am I to be tormented by that awful man?” she cried hysterically. “How dare you, sir, how could you venture to disturb a lady who is a stranger to you, in her own house at such an hour, and to force yourself upon her to talk of a man who came here, to this very drawing room, only three hours ago, to murder me, and went stamping out of the room, as no one would go out of a decent house. Let me tell you, sir, that I shall lodge a complaint against you—I will not let this pass. Kindly leave me at once. I am a mother. I—I—”
“Murder! Then he tried to murder you too?”
“Why, has he killed somebody else?” Madame Hohlakov asked impulsively.

“If you would kindly listen, madam, for half a moment, I'll explain it all in a couple of words,” answered Perhotin, firmly. “At five o'clock this afternoon Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know for a fact he had no money. Yet at nine o'clock, he came to see me with a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand—about two or three thousand roubles. His hands and face were all covered in blood, and he looked like a madman. When I asked him where he'd got so much money, he answered that he had just received it from you—that you had given him a sum of three thousand to go to the gold mines—”
Madame Hohlakov's face took on an expression of intense, painful excitement.
“Good God! He must have killed his old father!” she cried, clasping her hands. “I never gave him money, never! Oh, run, run! Don't say another word! Save the old man—run to his father—run!”
“Excuse me, madam, so you did not give him money? You remember for a fact that you did not give him any money?”

“No, I didn't, I didn't! I refused to give it to him, for he could not appreciate it. He ran out in a fury, stamping. He rushed at me, but I slipped away. And let me tell you, as I want to hide nothing from you now, he actually spat at me. Can you imagine that! But why are we standing? Ah, sit down.”
“Excuse me, I—”
“Or better, run, run, you must run and save the poor old man from an awful death!”
“But what if he has killed him already?”
“Ah, good heavens, yes! Then what are we to do now? What do you think we ought to do now?”

Meanwhile she had made Pyotr Ilyitch sit down and sat down herself, facing him. Briefly but fairly clearly, Pyotr Ilyitch told her the history of the affair—at least the part he had witnessed himself. He described his visit to Fenya too, and told her about the pestle. All these details had an overwhelming effect on the distracted lady, who kept letting out shrieks and covering her face with her hands.

“Would you believe it, I foresaw all of this! I have that special gift—whatever I imagine comes to pass. And how often I've looked at that awful man and always thought, that man will end by murdering me. And now it's happened—that is, if he hasn't murdered me, but only his own father, it's only because the finger of God preserved me, and what's more, he was ashamed to murder me because, in this very place, I put the holy ikon from the relics of the holy martyr, Saint Varvara, on his neck. And to think how close I was to death at that moment—I went right up to him, and he stretched out his neck toward me! Do you know, Pyotr Ilyitch (I think you said your name was Pyotr Ilyitch), I don't believe in miracles, but that ikon and this unmistakable miracle with me now—it shakes me, and I'm ready to believe in anything you like. Have you heard about Father Zossima? But I don't know what I'm saying—and just imagine, with the ikon on his neck he spat at me. He only spat, it's true, he didn't murder me, and—he dashed away! But what shall we do, what must we do now? What do you think?”
Pyotr Ilyitch stood up and announced that he was going straight to the police captain, to tell him everything, and leave him to do what he thought fit.

“Oh, he's an excellent man, excellent! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he's the person to go to. How practical you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! How well you've thought of everything! I would never have thought of it in your place!”

“Especially as I know the police captain very well myself,” remarked Pyotr Ilyitch, who was still standing and was obviously anxious to escape as quickly as possible from the impulsive lady, who wouldn't let him say goodbye and go.

“And be sure, be sure,” she prattled on, “to come back and tell me what you see there, and what you find out—what comes to light—how they'll try him—and what he's sentenced to. Tell me, we don't have capital punishment, do we? But be sure to come, even if it's at three o'clock in the morning, at four, at half past four. Tell them to wake me, to wake me, to shake me, if I don't get up. But, good heavens, I shan't sleep! But wait, hadn't I better come with you?”
“N—no. But if you would write three lines in your own hand, stating that you did not give Dmitri Fyodorovitch money, it might perhaps be useful—in case it's needed—”

“To be sure!” Madame Hohlakov skipped delightedly to her bureau. “And you know, I'm simply struck, amazed by your resourcefulness, your good sense in these affairs. Are you in the service here? I'm delighted to think you're in the service here!”
And still talking, she scribbled on half a sheet of notepaper the following lines:

I have never in my life lent to that unhappy man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, in spite of all, he is unhappy), three thousand roubles today. I have never given him money, never: That I swear by all that's holy!
K. HOHLAKOV.
“Here's the note!” she said, turning quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. “Go, save him. It's a noble deed on your part!”
And she made the sign of the cross three times over him. She ran out to accompany him to the passage.

“How grateful I am to you! You can't imagine how grateful I am that you came to me first. How is it we haven't met before? I shall feel flattered to see you at my house in the future. How delightful that you're living here! Such precision! Such practical ability! They must appreciate you, they must understand you. If there's anything I can do, believe me—oh, I love young people! I'm in love with young people! The younger generation is the one prop of our suffering country. Her one hope. Oh, go, go!”

But Pyotr Ilyitch had already hurried away, or she wouldn't have let him go so soon. Yet Madame Hohlakov had made a rather agreeable impression on him, which somewhat softened his anxiety about being drawn into such an unpleasant affair. Tastes differ, as we all know. “She's by no means so elderly,” he thought, feeling pleased. “On the contrary, I'd have taken her for her own daughter.”

As for Madame Hohlakov, she was simply enchanted by the young man. “Such sense! Such exactness! In so young a man! In our day! And all that with such manners and appearance! People say the young people of today are good for nothing, but here's an example!” and so on. So she simply forgot about this “dreadful affair,” and it was only as she was getting into bed that, suddenly recalling “how close she had been to death,” she exclaimed: “Ah, it is awful, awful!”
But she fell at once into a sound, sweet sleep.

I would not, however, have dwelt on such trivial and irrelevant details, had this eccentric meeting of the young official with the by no means elderly widow not later turned out to be the foundation of the whole career of that practical and precise young man. His story is remembered to this day with amazement in our town, and I shall perhaps have something to say about it once I have finished my long history of the Brothers Karamazov.
